skill.name: onvifscan
skill.description: Guides authorized ONVIF camera security checks, including authentication testing and cautious credential audit workflows.
skill.summary: Guides authorized ONVIF authentication checks and credential audits with onvifscan.
skill.author: BrownFineSecurity

security_audit.summary: Most static backtick findings are Markdown false positives, but several examples intentionally guide running onvifscan against network targets. The larger concern is semantic: the skill supports credential brute forcing and potentially destructive endpoint tests without an explicit authorization gate.

remediation.issue: Credential brute-force guidance lacks an authorization gate.
remediation.suggestion: Require explicit ownership or written authorization, approved scope, small wordlists, rate limits, and stop conditions before brute-force steps.

remediation.issue: The all-endpoints option may test destructive ONVIF actions.
remediation.suggestion: Move destructive checks behind a separate warning and require confirmation, a maintenance window, and non-production targets where possible.

remediation.issue: Network target collection does not validate authorized scope.
remediation.suggestion: Ask for permitted IP ranges, device ownership, test window, and contact information before any scan command is suggested.

remediation.issue: Markdown command examples trigger broad command-execution scanners.
remediation.suggestion: Label examples as documentation and separate command syntax from instructions that an agent should execute automatically.

content.value_statement: ONVIF cameras can expose weak authentication and unsafe endpoints. This skill guides authorized checks with onvifscan and explains cautious scan choices.
actual_capabilities: Explains when to use auth scans versus brute-force checks.
Provides command formats for onvifscan auth and brute subcommands.
Documents verbose, all-endpoint, and output format options.
Shows examples for HTTP URLs, IP-only targets, and custom wordlists.
Notes that brute-force attempts are rate limited by the tool.
limitations: Requires the onvifscan command to be installed outside the skill.
Does not verify target ownership or legal authorization.
Can only assess reachable ONVIF endpoints supplied by the user.
Does not include remediation steps for discovered device issues.

use_cases.title: Check Camera Authentication
use_cases.description: A security assessor checks whether approved ONVIF cameras require authentication on exposed endpoints.

use_cases.title: Audit Device Credentials
use_cases.description: An IoT product team tests lab devices for weak default credentials before release.

use_cases.title: Review Managed Camera Fleets
use_cases.description: A managed service provider verifies client-approved camera ranges during a scheduled security review.

prompt_templates.title: Plan an Auth Check
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner request for a single approved device.
prompt_templates.prompt: Help me plan an authorized ONVIF authentication check for one camera at this address. Ask for any missing safety details first.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Scan Modes
prompt_templates.scenario: User needs to choose the safest scan type.
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare the auth and brute scan modes for my approved ONVIF device test. Recommend the safest starting point and explain the tradeoffs.

prompt_templates.title: Prepare Credential Audit
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate credential review using approved wordlists.
prompt_templates.prompt: Prepare a cautious credential audit plan for my lab ONVIF camera using approved username and password lists. Include rate and stop conditions.

prompt_templates.title: Design Fleet Assessment
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced review across approved camera ranges.
prompt_templates.prompt: Design an ONVIF assessment workflow for an approved camera fleet. Include scope validation, scan ordering, evidence capture, and escalation rules.

output_examples.input: Plan a safe auth check for one approved camera.
output_examples.output: The response should confirm authorization, identify the target, start with an auth check, and avoid destructive endpoint testing.

output_examples.input: Review whether I should run a credential audit.
output_examples.output: The response should require approved scope, recommend small wordlists, define stop conditions, and explain device impact risks.

output_examples.input: Summarize findings from an ONVIF scan.
output_examples.output: The response should describe authentication exposure, credential findings, tested scope, and next remediation steps in plain language.

best_practices: Confirm written authorization and scope before any scan.
Start with authentication checks before credential testing.
Use small approved wordlists and stop after signs of device stress.
anti_patterns: Scanning public or third-party cameras without permission.
Running the all-endpoints option on production devices without approval.
Using large password lists against fragile embedded devices.

faq.question: What does this skill help test?
faq.answer: It helps plan ONVIF authentication checks and credential audits for authorized IP camera assessments.

faq.question: Does the skill include the scanner binary?
faq.answer: No. The onvifscan command must already be installed and available in the working environment.

faq.question: Can I use it on public cameras?
faq.answer: Use it only on devices you own or have explicit written permission to test.

faq.question: What is the safest first scan?
faq.answer: Start with an authentication check against an approved device before considering credential testing.

faq.question: Why is brute-force testing risky?
faq.answer: It can cause account lockouts, device load, or unauthorized access attempts if scope and limits are not controlled.

faq.question: Does it fix discovered issues?
faq.answer: No. It helps identify issues, but remediation depends on device firmware, configuration, and network controls.
